title: Enterprise Buyer Security Requirements: What to Prepare
summary: What enterprise buyers check in a B2B software vendor, which evidence they ask for, and how to answer security reviews faster without overclaiming.
body_markdown:
Enterprise buyers want three things from a software vendor's security review: documented controls, independent evidence that those controls exist, and answers that stay consistent from one questionnaire to the next. Vendors that hold all three in one maintained place close deals faster, because the review stops being a one-off scramble and becomes a repeatable process. This guide covers what buyers assess, the patterns in their questionnaires, the evidence they request, and how your security, compliance and sales teams can answer without overclaiming.

## TL;DR


- Buyers scope their review by data sensitivity, hosting model and jurisdiction, so expect a heavier review the closer you sit to regulated or personal data.
- The core of every review is the same: identity and access, encryption, logging, incident response, vulnerability management and subprocessors.
- Independent evidence (a current SOC 2 Type 2 report, ISO/IEC 27001 certification, a public trust center) carries more weight than adjectives.
- Questions that do not apply can be marked N/A, and a certificate never answers every question on its own, so map each answer to its source.
- A single maintained answer library, with owners and review dates, is what turns a two-week review into a same-day response.

## What enterprise buyers assess first


Most reviews begin before the questionnaire arrives. The buyer's security team decides how much scrutiny you deserve. HubSpot's software procurement checklist says[buyers should run security, privacy and compliance reviews alongside the functional evaluation](https://blog.hubspot.com/sales/software-procurement-checklist) , starting with what data the software handles, who uses it, where it is hosted and which legal or contractual obligations apply.


That intake step explains why two buyers send very different questionnaires to the same vendor. A marketing tool that touches no customer data may get a short form. A platform that stores financial records or deeply integrates into production systems will get the full treatment.


The areas that nearly every buyer covers fall into a few groups:


- **Identity and access:** Australia's Cyber Security Centre guide lists questions on[which identity and access management protocols a product supports and whether it offers SSO](https://www.cyber.gov.au/sites/default/files/2025-03/Choosing%20secure%20and%20verifiable%20technologies%20%28December%202024%29.pdf) .
- **Encryption:** the same guide asks what standards protect data at rest, in transit and in use.
- **Logging and monitoring:** buyers ask what is logged, for how long, and whether logs can be exported to their own tooling.
- **Incident response and vulnerability handling:** how you detect, notify and remediate, and whether you publish a disclosure policy.
- **Governance:** policies, certifications, personnel screening, subprocessors and data residency.


The same Australian guide states that procuring organizations must establish and document their security requirements in advance. In practice, that means your questionnaire answers are being scored against a written baseline, not read for general impressions.


## Product security versus company security


A useful shift in how US buyers think comes from CISA. Its[Secure by Demand Guide](https://www.cisa.gov/resources-tools/resources/secure-demand-guide) argues that procurement due diligence has focused heavily on enterprise security, meaning how the vendor protects its own infrastructure, while fewer standards address the security of the product itself.


For your team, this means two sets of questions. One set is about your company: policies, staff training, corporate network controls. The other is about what you ship. CISA's guide asks buyers to verify that manufacturers:


- support standards-based SSO at no additional cost;
- enable MFA, or phishing-resistant authentication such as passkeys, by default;
- have eliminated default passwords;
- file timely CVE records (public identifiers for known vulnerabilities) with accurate CWE and CPE fields;
- publish a public vulnerability disclosure policy.


It also points buyers to artifacts such as a machine-readable software bill of materials (SBOM, a list of the third-party components inside your product) and roadmaps showing plans to eliminate whole classes of vulnerabilities, for example memory-safety issues. For SaaS and cloud providers, the guide says customers should expect security logs to be retained and available for at least six months at no additional charge, covering configuration changes, identity events such as sign-in and token creation, and data access.


If you sell to security-mature buyers, expect some of these to appear in your questionnaires, and decide in advance who owns each answer.


## Patterns in enterprise security questionnaires


Questionnaires look different on the surface and repeat underneath. Vendors usually meet three shapes: standardized frameworks such as the CAIQ (from the Cloud Security Alliance) and the SIG (from Shared Assessments), and bespoke spreadsheets that encode a single buyer's own risk method. We cover how these formats differ, and the mistakes that cost vendors time, in[our guide to questionnaire formats](https://skypher.co/post/how-to-answer-security-questionnaires) .


CISA's[fact sheet on procuring safe and secure ICT products](https://www.cisa.gov/resources-tools/resources/procuring-safe-and-secure-ict-products-and-services-fact-sheet) offers a question template meant to illuminate risk factors for the specific product being acquired. It also notes that such questions help reduce risk rather than eliminate it. That framing matters: a questionnaire is a risk-reduction tool, so buyers read your answers for consistency and for evidence, not for perfection.


Three patterns show up again and again:


1. **The same control domains in different wording.** Access management, encryption, backup and recovery, logging, incident process, vulnerability management, personnel security, subprocessors and data residency recur across almost every format.
2. **Follow-up on the answer, not the question.** A "yes" to MFA is followed by "for all users, including administrators and support staff?"
3. **Requests for proof.** Answers are tied to a policy, a report or a screenshot.


The ISC2 article on[vendor security credentials](https://www.isc2.org/Insights/2026/06/vendor-security-credentials-and-functionality) shows how far this can go. In one practitioner's enterprise review, the buyer required documentation on data residency and legal jurisdictions, was not satisfied by SSO alone and asked for evidence of just-in-time provisioning and orphaned-account remediation, and required platform logs to be ingested into its own SIEM, the system its security operations team uses to monitor events. Plan for the second and third question behind every first one.


A 200-question spreadsheet therefore tends to contain perhaps a few dozen distinct ideas. Teams that recognize this answer once and reuse the answer everywhere.


## Evidence buyers ask you to hand over


Buyers increasingly separate claims from proof. The commonly requested set, drawn from HubSpot's checklist and the CISA guide, looks like this:


Evidence What it shows What buyers check


SOC 2 Type 2 report An auditor's assurance on controls at a service organization Report period, scope, exceptions


ISO/IEC 27001:2022 certificate An information security management system meets the international standard Scope statement, certifying body


Pen-test summary Recent independent testing of the product Date, scope, remediation status


Incident-response documentation How you detect, escalate and notify Written plan, notification terms


Uptime and SLA records Availability history Service-level commitments


SBOM and disclosure policy Component transparency and vulnerability handling Machine-readable format, public policy


Subprocessor list and DPA Who else touches the data, under what terms Currency, locations


HubSpot's checklist describes a[SOC 2 Type 2 report as an AICPA assurance report on controls](https://blog.hubspot.com/sales/software-procurement-checklist) and ISO/IEC 27001:2022 as the international standard for information security management systems. It adds that when a vendor publishes a trust center, buyers should treat it as a starting point and confirm that reports, certifications, subprocessor lists and policies are current and in scope.


That last point is where many vendors lose days. If the trust center is stale, the buyer asks for the documents by email, and the review restarts. Our[Trust Center](https://skypher.co/trust-center) is a customizable, customer-facing page for sharing your security and compliance posture, so the documents buyers look for first are already in front of them.


We also wrote a separate piece on[what proof to show buyers](https://blog.skypher.co/blog/saas-compliance-proof-for-buyers) , including how to present a report so it answers the question being asked.


### Make the report easy to trust


When you share a SOC 2 report, make sure the period is recent and the scope names the product the buyer is purchasing. If a gap exists between the end of the audit period and today, a bridge letter (a short statement from management covering the gap) answers the obvious question before it is asked. Brief the sales team so they can explain what the report covers in a sentence.


Independent evidence also supports the broader trust story. Our note on[website security and customer trust](https://babylovegrowth.ai/blog/importance-website-security) is a useful companion when you are deciding which assurance reports and certifications to put in front of buyers.


## How requirements change with the deal


Not every buyer asks for the same depth, and your team should not answer them all with the same effort. The ABA Cybersecurity Task Force's[vendor contracting checklist](https://www.eckertseamans.com/app/uploads/ABA_Cybersecurity-Task-Force-Vendor-Contracting-Checklist.pdf) says the scope of assessment should reflect the nature and importance of the product or service and the sensitivity of the information the vendor will collect, store, process or transmit, including personal data, financial information, protected health information, proprietary information and trade secrets. It also directs purchasers to consider the delivery model, subcontractors, and legal and regulatory requirements across jurisdictions.


Translate that into four questions to ask yourself about every opportunity:


1. **What data will we hold for this buyer?** Regulated or personal data raises the evidence bar.
2. **How deeply do we integrate?** A product with administrative access to production systems is reviewed more heavily than a standalone tool.
3. **Where is it hosted and who are our subprocessors?** Residency and jurisdiction questions follow.
4. **What does the buyer's industry require?** Financial services and healthcare buyers add sector-specific controls and due diligence questionnaires.


For investment managers and financial institutions, due diligence questionnaires (DDQs) add an extra layer.[Fiduciary-Grade DDQ Automation](https://skypher.co/automate-ddqs) is the part of Skypher built for that format.


## Handling gaps and questions that do not apply


No vendor meets every control a buyer lists. What matters is how you answer without making unsupported claims. NERC's[vendor risk management guideline](https://www.nerc.com/globalassets/who-we-are/standing-committees/rstc/scs/security_guideline-vendor_risk_management_lifecycle.pdf) is useful here, because it describes how the buyer side is meant to behave:


- Questions that do not apply to a vendor can be marked "N/A" so the vendor knows it need not answer them.
- Buyers should first check documents the vendor already publishes to see whether they answer questions.
- A certification such as ISO 27001 or SOC 2 may address many questions, but buyers should not accept it as answering every one without verifying where each question is addressed.
- Questionnaires should be provided at least annually.


For your team, this suggests a simple discipline:


- Answer what is asked, and mark what is genuinely out of scope as N/A with a one-line reason.
- When pointing to a certificate, name the section or control that answers the question, rather than attaching the whole report.
- When a control is partial, say what exists today and what is planned, with an owner and a date you can keep.
- Point to published documents first. If your trust center already answers the question, link to it.


The principle is evidence over adjectives. Saying you take security seriously earns nothing, while a precise answer tied to a document earns the buyer's confidence and shortens the follow-up thread.


## Build the answer process before the next review


The best response to varied requirements is a single, current source of truth. This is the routine we recommend, and where our platform takes work off your team.


1. **Collect your source material.** Policies, past questionnaires, audit reports and architecture notes belong in one knowledge base. Our platform connects to Confluence, Notion, Google Drive, OneDrive and SharePoint, so the content your teams already maintain stays the source.
2. **Organize answers by control domain.** Group them under access, encryption, logging, incident response, vulnerability management, personnel, subprocessors and residency. Each entry should hold a standard answer, a short version, a link to the policy and the matching evidence.
3. **Assign an owner and a review date to every answer.** Content management with document versioning in Skypher keeps track of what changed and when.
4. **Draft from the library, not from scratch.** Our proprietary retrieval AI drafts answers from your own content and returns a confidence score, so reviewers can focus on lower-confidence items. It parses every questionnaire format and is built to answer even 200 questions in under a minute.
5. **Route questions to the right expert.** Collaboration is real-time with unlimited users, and the Slack and MS Teams integrations (including chatbot support) let engineers answer where they already work.
6. **Deliver where the buyer asks for it.** Over 40 integrations with third-party risk management platforms and enterprise tools, including OneTrust and ServiceNow, mean answers can go into the buyer's portal without retyping.
7. **Publish what you can proactively.** Put current reports and policies in your Trust Center so that many questions never reach you.
8. **Review after every submission.** Feed corrected or newly approved answers back into the library so the next buyer benefits.


For more on the process, see our guides on[how to answer security questionnaires effectively](https://skypher.co/post/how-to-answer-security-questionnaires-en) and[how to respond to an RFP security questionnaire](https://blog.skypher.co/blog/how-to-respond-to-an-rfp) .

## FAQ


### What security requirements do enterprise buyers ask software vendors about most often?


The common core is identity and access management (including SSO and MFA), encryption at rest and in transit, logging, incident response, vulnerability management, subprocessors and data residency. Buyers then add depth according to the sensitivity of the data you will handle and how deeply your product integrates.


### Does a SOC 2 report or ISO 27001 certificate answer the whole questionnaire?


It answers many questions, but buyers are advised to verify where each question is addressed and to request answers for anything the certification does not cover. Map each answer to the relevant control or report section, and keep the report period current.


### Can we mark questions as not applicable?


Yes. Official guidance from NERC says questions that do not apply to a vendor can be marked N/A so the vendor knows it need not answer them. Add a short reason so the buyer's reviewer can confirm the scope.


### How can we answer faster without lowering quality?


Keep one maintained library of approved answers organized by control domain, with an owner and review date for each. Draft from that library, send low-confidence items to the right expert, and publish current documents in a trust center so repeated questions are answered before they are asked.
